outcomes.title: L'Hopitals Rule
outcomes.description: Apply L'Hopitals Rule when appropriate to evaluate limits.
outcomes.template:
Evaluate the following limits. Identify any infinite limits by their signs. Only apply L'Hopitals rule when valid.

\renewcommand{\log}{\ln} \displaystyle \lim_{x\to {{a}}^{ {{directionsymbol}} } } {{fx}} .

\renewcommand{\log}{\ln} \displaystyle \lim_{x\to {{a}}^{ {{directionsymbol}} } } {{fx}} = {{thelimit}} .

outcomes.title: Rates of Vanishing
outcomes.description: Determine the rate at which a function vanishes.
outcomes.template:
Suppose that \renewcommand{\log}{\ln} \displaystyle \lim_{x\to {{a}}^{ {{directionsymbol}} }} \frac{ {{fx}} }{ x^p } is well defined, not zero, nor infinite. Find p and this limit.

\renewcommand{\log}{\ln}\displaystyle \lim_{x\to {{a}}^{ {{directionsymbol}} }} \frac{ {{fx}} }{ {{gx}} } = {{thelimit}} .

outcomes.title: Integration by Parts
outcomes.description: Find the integral of a function using integration by parts (and substitution when appropriate).
outcomes.template:
Solve the following integrals.

\renewcommand{\log}{\ln} \displaystyle \int_{ {{a1}} }^{ {{b1}} } {{fx}}dx.

\renewcommand{\log}{\ln} \displaystyle \int_{ {{a1}} }^{ {{b1}} } {{fx}}dx = {{Int1}}.

\renewcommand{\log}{\ln} \displaystyle \int {{gx}}dx.

By letting \renewcommand{\log}{\ln} u={{U}}, we have that \renewcommand{\log}{\ln} dx = {{dx}}du. Then by applying parts to the u integral we obtain: \renewcommand{\log}{\ln} \displaystyle \int {{gx}}dx = {{Int2}}+C.

outcomes.title: Integral of Trigonometric Functions
outcomes.description: Find the integral of trigonometric functions using identities, parts and/or substitution.
outcomes.template:
Solve the following integrals. Note that there are many ways to write the same trig expression via identities. Recall that \displaystyle \sin^2(\theta) = \frac{1 - \cos(2\theta)}{2}, \cos^2(\theta) = \frac{1 + \cos(2\theta)}{2}.

\renewcommand{\log}{\ln} \displaystyle \int_{ {{a}} }^{ {{b}} } {{fx}}dx.

\renewcommand{\log}{\ln} \displaystyle \int {{fx}}dx.

\renewcommand{\log}{\ln} \displaystyle \int_{ {{a}} }^{ {{b}} } {{fx}}dx = \left({{Fx}}\right)\Big|_{ {{a}} }^{ {{b}} } ={{Int}}.

\renewcommand{\log}{\ln} \displaystyle \int {{fx}}dx = {{Fx}} +C.

outcomes.title: Trigonometric Substitution
outcomes.description: Find the integral of algebraic functions via trigonometric substitution.
outcomes.template:
Solve the following integrals. Note that there are many ways to write the same trig expression via identities.

\renewcommand{\log}{\ln} \displaystyle \int_{ {{lowx}} }^{ {{highx}} } {{fx}}dx.

\renewcommand{\log}{\ln} \displaystyle \int {{fx}}dx.

By letting x = {{sub}}, we obtain: \renewcommand{\log}{\ln} \displaystyle \int_{ {{lowx}} }^{ {{highx}} } {{fx}}dx = \int_{ {{lowt}} }^{ {{hight}} } {{ft}}d\theta =\left({{Ft}}\right)\Big|_{ {{lowt}} }^{ {{hight}} } ={{Int}}.

By letting x = {{sub}}, we obtain: \renewcommand{\log}{\ln} \displaystyle \int {{fx}}dx = \int {{ft}}d\theta = {{Ft}} +C ={{Fx}} +C.

outcomes.title: Partial Fractions
outcomes.description: Find the integral of rational functions via partial fraction decomposition.
outcomes.template:
Solve the following integrals using partial fraction decomposition and substitution when appropriate.

\renewcommand{\log}{\ln} \displaystyle \int \frac{ {{num}} }{ {{denom}} } dx.

Since \renewcommand{\log}{\ln} \displaystyle \frac{ {{num}} }{ {{denom}} } = {{PF}} We have that \renewcommand{\log}{\ln} \displaystyle \int \frac{ {{num}} }{ {{denom}} } dx = \int \left( {{PF}} \right)dx = {{Fx}} +C .

\renewcommand{\log}{\ln} \displaystyle \int {{f2x}}dx.

By letting \renewcommand{\log}{\ln} u={{U}}, we have that \renewcommand{\log}{\ln} \displaystyle \int {{f2x}}dx = {{F2x}}+C.

outcomes.title: Improper Integrals as Limits
outcomes.description: Write an improper integral as the limit of a proper definite integral to compute the value.
outcomes.template:
Express the following improper integrals as the (sum of) limit(s) of proper integral(s), and compute the integrals.

\renewcommand{\log}{\ln} \displaystyle \int_{ {{left}} }^{ {{right}} } {{fx}}dx.

Note that \renewcommand{\log}{\ln} \displaystyle \int {{fx}}dx ={{Fx}} +C.

Thus \renewcommand{\log}{\ln} \displaystyle \int_{ {{left}} }^{ {{right}} } {{fx}} dx = \lim_{c\to {{left}}^+ } \left( {{Fx}} \right)\Big|_{c}^{ {{right}} } = {{Int}}. \renewcommand{\log}{\ln} \displaystyle \int_{ {{left}} }^{ {{right}} } {{fx}} dx = \lim_{c\to \infty } \left( {{Fx}} \right)\Big|_{ {{left}} }^{ c } = {{Int}}. \renewcommand{\log}{\ln} \displaystyle \int_{ {{left}} }^{ {{right}} } {{fx}} dx = \displaystyle \int_{ {{left}} }^{ 1 } {{fx}} dx + \displaystyle \int_{ 1 }^{ {{right}} } {{fx}} dx = \lim_{c_1\to 0^+ } \left( {{Fx}} \right)\Big|_{ c_1 }^{ 1 } +\lim_{c_2\to \infty } \left( {{Fx}} \right)\Big|_{ 1 }^{ c_2 } = \left({{Int1}}\right) + \left({{Int2}}\right) = {{Int}} .

outcomes.title: Improper Integrals via p-test and Comparison Theorem
outcomes.description: Use  the p-test and the Comparison Theorem for integrals to determine if an improper integral converges.
outcomes.template:
Use legitimate inequalities and the p-test to determine if an improper integral converges.

\renewcommand{\log}{\ln} \displaystyle \int_{ {{start }} }^\infty {{fx}}dx.

\renewcommand{\log}{\ln} \displaystyle \int_0^1 {{fx}}dx.

Note that for x\geq {{start}}, we have that \displaystyle 0\leq \frac{ \sqrt{ {{T11}} + {{T12}} + {{T14}} +{{T13}} } }{ {{T21}} + {{T22}} + {{T24}} +{{T23}} } \leq \frac{ \sqrt{ {{t11}} + {{t12}} + {{t14}} +{{t13}} } }{ {{t21}} } \frac{ {{T11}} + {{T12}} + {{T14}} +{{T13}} }{ \sqrt{ {{T21}} + {{T22}} + {{T24}} +{{T23}} } }\leq \frac{ {{t11}} + {{t12}} + {{t14}} +{{t13}} }{ \sqrt{ {{t21}} } } = {{simp}}. Thus \displaystyle \int_{ {{start }} }^\infty {{fx}}dx \leq \int_{ {{start }} }^\infty {{simp}}dx which converges since {{P}} > 1 . Thus \renewcommand{\log}{\ln} \displaystyle \int_{ {{start }} }^\infty {{fx}}dx converges as well by the Comparison Theorem. \displaystyle \frac{ \sqrt{ {{T11}} + {{T12}} + {{T14}} +{{T13}} } }{ {{T21}} + {{T22}} + {{T24}} +{{T23}} } \geq \frac{ \sqrt{ {{t11}} } }{ {{t21}} +{{t22}} +{{t24}} +{{t23}} } \frac{ {{T11}} + {{T12}} + {{T14}} +{{T13}} }{ \sqrt{ {{T21}} + {{T22}} + {{T24}} +{{T23}} } }\geq \frac{ {{t11}} }{ \sqrt{ {{t21}} +{{t22}} + {{t24}} +{{t23}} } } = {{simp}}\geq 0. Thus \displaystyle \int_{ {{start }} }^\infty {{fx}}dx \geq \int_{ {{start }} }^\infty {{simp}}dx which diverges since {{P}} \leq 1 . Thus \renewcommand{\log}{\ln} \displaystyle \int_{ {{start }} }^\infty {{fx}}dx diverges as well by the Comparison Theorem.
